topic: The word 'guy' comes from Guy Fawkes
pillar: Present: how things got this way (timely: Bonfire Night, 5 Nov)

claims.claim: In 1605 Guy Fawkes guarded the gunpowder (commonly given as 36 barrels) hidden in the undercroft beneath the House of Lords.
claims.note: Most sources give 36; a few say 'about 30'. 36 is the standard figure.

claims.claim: The plot aimed to blow up Parliament and King James I.
An anonymous warning letter (to Lord Monteagle) exposed the plot and Fawkes was caught with the gunpowder on the night of 4-5 November 1605.
Londoners lit bonfires in 1605 to celebrate the king's survival; burning effigies of Fawkes came later.
'Guy' meant an effigy of Guy Fawkes (OED first citation 1806), then a grotesquely/poorly dressed person (1836), then any man/fellow (1847).
claims.note: OED says the earliest 'man' examples 'may be influenced' by the effigy sense; etymonline and Ayto state the link. Script describes the chain, does not claim certainty beyond it.

rejected.claim: The first 1605 bonfires burned Guy Fawkes effigies.
rejected.reason: Wrong - they celebrated the king; effigies came later.
